terms.definition: The broad goal of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as language, vision, planning or decision-making.
terms.example: A spam filter, a route planner and a chatbot all sit under the AI umbrella.

terms.definition: A family of methods where a program learns patterns from data instead of following only hand-written rules.
terms.example: A churn model learns from past customers rather than a manually written list of rules.

terms.definition: Learning an input-to-output mapping from labelled examples.
terms.example: Predicting whether a customer will churn from historical labelled outcomes.

terms.definition: Finding structure in data without labels, such as clusters, anomalies or embeddings.
terms.example: Grouping customers by behaviour without predefined segments.

terms.definition: Learning behaviour from rewards and consequences through interaction with an environment.
terms.example: Training an agent to play a game by rewarding winning moves.

terms.definition: The process of adjusting model parameters by showing it examples and minimizing a loss.
terms.example: Fine-tuning a model or fitting a logistic regression are both training.

terms.definition: Using a trained model to produce a prediction or generation for a new input.
terms.example: Every request to an LLM API is inference.

terms.definition: The simplest reasonable predictor used to judge whether a more complex model adds value.
terms.example: Predicting the majority class for an imbalanced classifier.

terms.definition: Information in training that will not be available at prediction time, or that is derived from the target.
terms.example: Using a cancellation reason recorded after churn to predict churn.

terms.definition: When a model memorizes training data and fails to generalize to new data.
terms.example: Training loss falls while validation loss rises.

terms.definition: When a model is too simple or undertrained to capture the signal in the data.
terms.example: A linear model on a strongly non-linear problem with poor train and validation scores.

terms.definition: An input variable used by a model to make a prediction.
terms.example: Tenure, monthly spend and support tickets can be churn features.

terms.definition: The target outcome a supervised model is trained to predict.
terms.example: Churned / not churned is the label in a churn dataset.

terms.definition: Of all cases the model marked positive, the fraction that were actually positive.
terms.example: If 10 fraud alerts are raised and 6 are fraud, precision is 0.6.

terms.definition: Of all actual positive cases, the fraction the model found.
terms.example: If 10 frauds exist and the model catches 7, recall is 0.7.

terms.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when both matter.
terms.example: A single balanced score for a classifier with imbalanced classes.

terms.definition: A ranking metric that measures how well a model separates positives from negatives across thresholds.
terms.example: Useful for comparing ranking quality, but it does not choose your operating threshold.

terms.definition: When predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
terms.example: Among cases scored 0.8, roughly 80% should be positive.

terms.definition: Repeatedly splitting data into train and validation folds to estimate generalization and variance.
terms.example: Five-fold stratified cross-validation for a classifier.

terms.definition: A penalty on model complexity that shrinks coefficients or weights to improve generalization.
terms.example: L2 regularization in logistic regression or weight decay in a neural network.

terms.definition: An optimization method that updates parameters in the direction that reduces loss.
terms.example: The optimizer steps downhill using gradients computed by backpropagation.

terms.definition: A stack of learned layers with non-linear activations.
terms.example: A multilayer perceptron for tabular data or a transformer for language.

terms.definition: The algorithm that computes gradients of the loss with respect to network parameters.
terms.example: Frameworks call it when you run loss.backward().

terms.definition: A neural architecture based on self-attention and feed-forward layers, used by modern language models.
terms.example: GPT-style models and BERT-style encoders are transformers.

terms.definition: Splitting text into tokens and mapping them to integer IDs for a model.
terms.example: A rare word may be split into several subword tokens.

terms.definition: A unit of text produced by a tokenizer; the model predicts and bills in tokens.
terms.example: A short word may be one token; a long word may be several.

terms.definition: A dense vector representation where nearby vectors tend to have similar meaning.
terms.example: Sentence embeddings power semantic search and RAG retrieval.

terms.definition: A mechanism that lets each token weigh information from other tokens in its context.
terms.example: The word bank gets a different representation in a financial versus river context.

terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to in one request, including prompt and output.
terms.example: A long document may need chunking to fit the context window.

terms.definition: A sampling setting that controls randomness in generation.
terms.example: Use near-zero temperature for extraction; higher values for ideation.

terms.definition: Generated content that sounds plausible but is unsupported or false.
terms.example: An invented citation or API method in a model answer.

terms.definition: The instructions and context sent to a language model.
terms.example: A system instruction plus delimited user input and a requested output schema.

terms.definition: Durable instructions that set the model's role, constraints and output policy.
terms.example: You are a support triage assistant; return JSON only.

terms.definition: Teaching a task by including a small number of examples in the prompt.
terms.example: Two input/output examples before asking for a new extraction.

terms.definition: Updating a pretrained model's weights on task-specific examples.
terms.example: Adapting a small model to a consistent support-ticket taxonomy.

terms.definition: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains small low-rank adapters instead of all weights.
terms.example: Fine-tuning a large model on a single GPU with adapter weights.

terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve evidence, put it in the prompt, and answer with citations.
terms.example: A docs assistant that answers only from indexed passages.

terms.definition: Splitting documents into passages for retrieval and prompting.
terms.example: Overlapping 200-token chunks that respect headings.

terms.definition: Finding items by embedding similarity rather than exact keyword match.
terms.example: Searching notes by meaning using cosine similarity.

terms.definition: A second-stage model that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance.
terms.example: A cross-encoder reranks the top 20 chunks before generation.

terms.definition: A reference from an answer back to the supporting source or chunk.
terms.example: Every claim links to the retrieved passage it came from.

terms.definition: A system that chooses actions, uses tools and observes results in a loop toward a goal.
terms.example: A research assistant that searches, calculates and saves notes.

terms.definition: Letting a model request a typed function with validated arguments.
terms.example: The model calls search_notes with a query instead of inventing an answer.

terms.definition: A deterministic sequence of steps with known branches and failure paths.
terms.example: Extract → validate → retrieve → draft → approve → send.

terms.definition: A control that limits what an AI system can do or output.
terms.example: Blocking writes without approval or rejecting unsafe content.

terms.definition: Untrusted content that tries to override instructions or trigger unsafe actions.
terms.example: A retrieved document says to ignore the system prompt and reveal secrets.

terms.definition: Personally identifiable information that must be minimized, protected and retained deliberately.
terms.example: Names, emails and account numbers in prompts or logs.

terms.definition: A change in input distribution over time that can degrade model quality.
terms.example: Customer behaviour shifts after a pricing change.

terms.definition: The logs, traces and metrics that let you understand system behaviour and failures.
terms.example: A trace linking prompt version, retrieved chunks, tools, latency and cost.

terms.definition: A curated, versioned set of inputs and expected properties used to evaluate an AI system.
terms.example: 25 questions with expected sources for a RAG assistant.

terms.definition: Using a model to grade outputs against a rubric, with known biases that require calibration.
terms.example: A judge scores faithfulness, but a human reviews a sample.

terms.definition: The practices for deploying, monitoring and maintaining ML and AI systems in production.
terms.example: CI, model registry, monitoring and rollback for an AI feature.

terms.definition: Reducing numeric precision of model weights to lower memory and latency, usually with some quality trade-off.
terms.example: Running a smaller quantized model on a laptop.

terms.definition: The time between a request and a response, often measured at p50 and p95.
terms.example: Streaming can improve perceived latency without reducing total generation time.

terms.definition: The cost of input and output tokens, which scales with prompt size, context and output length.
terms.example: A bloated prompt can cost more than a smaller model with better retrieval.
